newsitem.title: USA: American Skiing Co. raises East's profile.
newsitem.headline: American Skiing Co. raises East's profile.

text.p: Think of skiing and the image of Colorodo's Rockies comes to mind. But for American Skiing Co., it's the East, with its New England ski resorts that is the center of the skiing universe.

American Skiing, the largest ski resort operator in the United States following a merger this summer, hopes to boost the world-wide profile of Vermont, New Hampshire and Maine ski areas with an aggressive marketing campaign.
The company also hopes the campaign raises the profile of its snowmaking equipment.
"There's a strong bias toward thinking that the world revolves around Colorado," ASC Chief Executive and owner Les Otten said in his office at Sunday River ski resort in Newry, Maine.
Otten's investments in snowmaking equipment have been recognized, at least within the industry, for creating skiing conditions that rival those in Colorado.

He hopes the $137 million July merger between Otten's LBO Enterprises and S-K-I Ltd. creating American Skiing Co. will help spread that message. The merger ended the regional rivalry between Killington and Sugarbush in Vermont and Sunday River and Sugarloaf USA in Maine and allowed the resorts to combine their marketing muscle against the Western giants Vail Resorts Inc. and Intrawest Corp.

ASC now controls eight ski resorts in Vermont, Maine and New Hampshire, and this year expects gross revenues of more than $200 million and about 3.5 million skier days -- the standard industry measure accounting for one skier skiing all or part of one day.
ASC has teamed up with major corporate sponsors to increase its marketing budget. It has also joined with British travel agents and Amtrak to bring more skiiers to the region.
"Two years ago, there wasn't a ski resort company on the continent that could create programs on the scale we're doing this winter," vice president of marketing Chris Brink said.

More Britains are now considering ski vacations in the Northeast United States, Otten said. This season, chartered flights direct from London to Bangor, Maine, will aid in bringing the 80,000 pre-booked skier visits from Britain, about 2.2 percent of this year's projected total.
Next year, charter air service from London will be offered to Burlington, Vt., Otten said. More than 150,000 skier days have been booked from Britain for next year already, he said.
The company is now broadening its scope to try to lure skiiers from Scandinavia, Continental Europe, South America and South Africa in coming years.
ASC is also reaching out to regional skiers.
"A lot of our skiiers leave the East to go skiing," he said. "We're closer to the market, it's cheaper to get here, we're in everybody's backyard."

ASC's growth coincides with industry consolidation. Vail Resorts may actually be larger than ASC following its merger with Ralcorp Holdings Inc.'s ski properties. But the U.S. Justice Department is reviewing that merger and may order Vail to sell some resorts, just as it told ASC to sell two New Hampshire resorts.

This month, rail line Amtrak began offering $99 round-trip tickets from New York to Rutland, Vt., a short distance from ASC resorts Killington, Pico, Sugarbush, Mount Snow or Haystack. The "Ethan Allen" express makes the trip in less than five hours, less time than it takes to drive.
"We forget that there are a lot of New Yorkers who don't have drivers licenses or access to cars," Otten said.
Last year ASC spent $18 million, with just $2 million spent by its promotional partners.

ASC's marketing budget this year will climb to more than $32 million, including $12 million to $14 million chipped in by its promotional partners including Visa, Pepsi and Mobil. ASC is now seen regularly in the eastern market on television, billboards and heard on the radio.
"Out West should be looked at as an alternative to Eastern skiing, not necessarily the savior of Eastern skiing," Otten said.
